event: Monday of week four: you wake in 15 again, Bea already up and pulling on running tights.
"Run," she says. "Monday. You've gone soft on swimming." You run the shore with her, twenty minutes.
Twenty minutes at her slow pace, and you finish it; Bea whoops and makes you do the last bit again.
At breakfast the post is out in the pigeonholes; Lin stands at hers with a thin blue envelope.
She reads it standing up, very still, and then folds it small and puts it in her skirt pocket.
At the table her porridge goes cold; when you ask, she says "My mother," very quietly, and stops.
Ten: the Foundations lecture in the Long Room; Lin sits beside you, her hands in her lap.
Her pen is always moving; today it lies still. You rest your hand on her knee, and she lets it stay.
Two: the Practice Hall; a candle on every bench, lit, and a new sigil on the board: the ward.
The demonstrator: a faint shell drawn round a flame to still it, so a draught can't touch it.
Kit walks past the end bench, and takes a middle one, between you and Amara, in full view.
She looks at you once along the bench, and breathes out, and turns to her candle.
Your ward goes round the flame like a soap bubble; the flame bends in the draught, then holds.
Bea's candle goes out entirely; she relights it with a match and a black look, twice.
Kit draws the ward with Amara watching openly; her hand slows, and goes on; the flame stands still.
It stands perfectly still, a gold drop in the draught from the high windows; the demonstrator stops.
"Ashworth," she says. "Good." Kit keeps her eyes on her flame, and her ears go scarlet.
Amara stares at Kit's flame, and then at Kit, and something in her face changes. "Oh," she says.
"That's why the end bench," Amara says, low. Kit's jaw sets. Amara says: "That's brave, Ashworth."
Kit looks at her, astonished. Amara turns back to her own candle, and her own ward wobbles.
Lin's ward is perfect, a fine clear shell, but her face is somewhere else entirely.
After practical, Lin touches your sleeve. "Will you come up? To 8? I need to show you something."
Room 8: drawings on every wall; she sits on the bed and takes out the blue letter and unfolds it.
"My mother writes every Monday. In Cantonese." She reads it to you in English, slowly.
The restaurant is busy; her father's back is bad; her sister is in London; and then the last line.
"She asks if I've told the academy yet. That I'm only staying the one year. Then home."
You look at her. Lin looks at the letter. "They expect it. I never said no. I never said anything."
"I thought I'd go back," she says. "Before I came. I thought one year would be enough. It isn't."
She looks round at her walls: the fells, the heron, the hands, the mere, the girls on the quad.
"What do you want?" you ask her. Whose wanting, you think. Lin's eyes fill.
"I want to stay," she says. "To draw. To finish. To be here." A breath. "With you."
You hold her while she cries, quietly, the way she does everything, charcoal on her fingers.
"I don't know how to tell them," she says. "Dad's back. The restaurant. I'm the one who stays home."
You say today she need only tell herself. Them later. She nods against your shoulder.
After a while she gets up and takes a folder from under her bed: the nine drawings from Thursday.
"I can look at them now," Lin says. She lays them out on the floor, one by one, all nine.
They are you, nude on the dais in lamplight; quick, sure, alive; your body seen whole and kindly.
In one you're looking straight at the artist. At her. Lin touches it. "You looked at me. Then."
You kneel on the floor among them and find you're blushing, and smiling, and can't stop either.
"Would you sit for me?" Lin asks. "Here. Now. Just for me." A pause. "Not clothed. This time."
You say yes. You undress in her room, in the low afternoon light, and sit on her window seat.
She draws you for an hour, slowly; this time you watch her the whole time, and she lets you.
When the light goes she puts the charcoal down and comes and kneels in front of the window seat.
She touches your bare knee with a charcoal fingertip, and leaves a small grey mark, and looks up.
She kisses you, slowly, her hands on your bare waist; you kiss her back, and she trembles.
"Soon," Lin says against your mouth. "I want to. Soon. When I'm not crying." You laugh, together.
You dress; she keeps the drawing, and pins it on the wall over her bed, in the middle of everything.
Evening: Priya bursts into the kitchen after charmcraft with oil on her face and her eyes huge.
"Amara held my hand," she says, to the room. "In the basement. Under the bench. With the clockwork."
Bea drops a spoon. Priya sits down very suddenly. "I have to ring Dev," she says. "I have to."
She goes out to ring him; she comes back an hour later, pale and calm, and says she's done it.
Bea makes her cocoa and sits with her; you sit on her other side; Priya says she feels light.
At eleven Lin knocks on 15; she has a letter in her hand, in pencil, half-written, in English.
"To my mother," she says. "I haven't sent it. I wrote it. That's the first thing." Bea makes room.
The three of you sit on Bea's bed while Lin reads it aloud in a whisper: I want to stay.
Lin sleeps in her own room; you sleep in 15, Bea warm at your back, charcoal still on your knee.
A day at Hollowmere ends.
